The '''Neue Staatsgalerie''' in [[Stuttgart]], [[Germany]], was designed by the British firm [[James Stirling (architect)|James Stirling]], Michael Wilford and Associates, although largely accredited solely to partner [[James Stirling (architect)|James Stirling]].  It was constructed between 1979 and 1984. The building has been claimed as the [[epitome]] of [[Postmodern architecture|Post-modernism]].

==Description==
[[Image:Staatsgalerie fg01.jpg|thumb|right|Distinctive rubber flooring in the foyer]]
The new gallery occupies a site next to the old [[Staatsgalerie Stuttgart|Staatsgalerie]]. A car park is located below the building. The building incorporates warm, natural elements of travertine and sandstone in classical forms, to contrast with the industrial pieces of green steel framing system and the bright pink and blue steel handrails. The architect intended to unite the monumental with the informal.<ref name="Museum Buildings" />

The building's most prominent feature is a central open-top rotunda.  This outdoor, enclosed space houses the sculpture garden.  It is circumnavigated by a public footpath and ramp that leads pedestrians through the site.  This feature allows the public to reach the higher elevation behind the museum from the lower front of the building's main face.<ref name="Museum Buildings" />

==History==
[[Image:Staatsgalerie1.jpg|thumb|left|Main entrance]]
The Neue Staatsgalerie was designed after Stirling and Wilford won a limited entry competition in 1977. It was constructed between 1979 and 1984.<ref name="Museum Buildings">{{Citation| last1 = von Naredi-Rainer |first1 = Paul|last2 = Hilger |first2 = Oliver|title = Museum Buildings: A Design Manual|url = https://books.google.com/books?id=yd6jhiw_ByAC&dq=Neue+Staatsgalerie&pg=PA70 |place = Basel  |publisher = [[Birkhäuser Verlag|Birkhäuser]] |pages = 70–72|year = 2004|isbn = 3-7643-6580-3 }}</ref> Located next-door to Stuttgart's [[Staatsgalerie Stuttgart|Alte Staatsgalerie]], the design echoed the neoclassical design of the older building. Elements also alluded to Stirling's earlier, unbuilt designs, as well as making reference to the [[Altes Museum]] in Berlin, the [[Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum|Guggenheim Museum]] in New York and the [[Pantheon, Rome|Pantheon]] in Rome.<ref name="Museum Buildings" />

By uniting Modernist elements with overt Classicism, architectural critic Charles Jencks claims the gallery "epitomized the first stage of [[Postmodern architecture|Post-Modernism]] in much the way the [[Villa Savoye]] and [[Barcelona Pavilion]] summarized early [[International style (architecture)|Modernism]]".<ref name="New Paradigm">{{Citation| last1 = Jencks |first1 = Charles |title = The New Paradigm in Architecture: The Language of Post-Modernism|url = https://books.google.com/books?id=20bkru0gzCMC&dq=Neue+Staatsgalerie&pg=PA110 |publisher = [[Yale University Press]] |pages = 110|year = 2002|isbn = 978-0300095135 }}</ref>
